title: A finitely generated ideal contained in the radical of I has a power contained in I

standard_prerequisites.name: Expansion of a power of a sum of s elements
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Standard multinomial expansion, used at the last step of the counted proof (line 6532)
standard_prerequisites.use: Shows that every monomial of degree n = d_1 + ... + d_s + 1 in the generators f_i has one exponent at least d_i, hence lies in I.

standard_prerequisites.name: Membership in the radical, read generator by generator
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: The hypothesis J contained in the radical of I, applied at proof line 6531
standard_prerequisites.use: Supplies, for each of the finitely many generators f_i of J, an exponent d_i with f_i^{d_i} in I.

core_obligations: Because J is finitely generated, say J = (f_1, ..., f_s), the hypothesis J contained in the radical of I can be unwound generator by generator into finitely many exponents d_i with f_i^{d_i} in I (proof line 6531).
Choose n = d_1 + ... + d_s + 1; every monomial of degree n in the f_i has some exponent at least d_i and therefore lies in I, so J^n is contained in I (proof lines 6530-6532).

Deduce the second assertion: in a Noetherian ring the nilradical is the radical of the zero ideal, so applying the first part with I = 0 turns an ideal all of whose elements are nilpotent into a nilpotent ideal (statement lines 6524-6526).
proof_roadmap: Write J as generated by finitely many elements and pick one exponent per generator from the radical hypothesis (proof lines 6530-6531).
Take n one larger than the sum of those exponents and read off that J^n is contained in I (proof line 6532).
difficulty_reason: For a Noetherian ring R and ideals I, J with J contained in the radical of I, the lemma asserts the existence of an exponent n with J^n contained in I, and consequently that locally nilpotent ideals are nilpotent in the Noetherian case (statement lines 6516-6527). The proof does not iterate powers of J or invoke primary decomposition: it unwinds the radical membership on the finitely many generators of J to get exponents d_i, and then takes n = d_1 + ... + d_s + 1, the length at which every monomial in the generators is forced to contain one f_i to the power d_i (proof lines 6529-6533). The finite generation of J is what makes this possible, and that is exactly where the Noetherian hypothesis enters; the author writes the whole argument out in three sentences. H2.
